title: Control systems
note: A controller drives a process variable toward a setpoint. Open-loop control acts without measuring the result; closed-loop (feedback) control measures the output, computes the error (setpoint minus output), and acts to shrink it. A PID controller adds terms proportional to the present error, its accumulated past, and its rate of change.

read.title: Measure, compare, correct
text: A toaster set to two minutes is an open-loop controller. It applies heat for a fixed time and never checks the bread. If the bread starts frozen, it comes out pale. A home thermostat is different: it measures room temperature, compares it with the setpoint, and turns the furnace on or off to shrink the error. That loop of measuring, comparing, and correcting is feedback, and it lets a system cope with disturbances its designers never predicted.

Most industrial loops use a PID controller. The proportional term pushes harder the larger the present error. Alone it often leaves a small permanent offset, so the integral term adds up past error and keeps pushing until the offset is gone. The derivative term watches how fast the error is changing and brakes the response before it overshoots, though it amplifies sensor noise.

Tuning is a balance. Too little gain gives a sluggish response; too much gives overshoot, oscillation, and in the worst case instability, where the output swings ever wider. Engineers judge a response by its rise time, overshoot, settling time, and steady-state error.
